interactive.title: A chord on a graph
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in twelve small screens on one graph. A function f(x) takes a number x and gives one back, and its graph plots each point (x, f(x)), with x across in seconds or minutes and f(x) up in metres or litres. Two points, P and Q, sit on the graph and can be dragged along it. A straight line, the chord, joins them, and a right-angled triangle under it shows the change between them, Δx across and Δy up, each labelled with its unit. The readout shows Δy ÷ Δx in units, which is the chord's slope. First a boat moving steadily away from a buoy, 4 m every second, so f(x) = 4x metres after x seconds. Dragging P or Q changes Δx and Δy together and the readout stays at 4 m per s, because every second adds the same 4 m. Then the line bends into a boat speeding up from the quay, f(x) = x² metres, where x² means x × x. It covers 1, 3, 5 and 7 m in its first four seconds, more each second, so the readout changes as the points move. Both graphs pass through (0, 0) and (4 s, 16 m), so the chord from 0 to 4 s reads 4 m per s on both. A draining tank, f(x) = 2(10 − x)² litres after x minutes, gives a falling graph, a Δy below zero and a minus rate; its values are labelled on the points so no working with the rule is needed. Two screens show example readings in a small table, plotted as dots, with the chord drawn between the two rows used. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it: a puzzle offers three answers, and a wrong pick is shown going wrong on the triangle.
interactive.ignores: The boats' and the tank's rules are example rules chosen to keep the numbers whole, and the table readings are example figures, not from a real motor, capacitor or tank. Real readings wobble a little; the graphs here are smooth. The chord depends only on where its two points are, so a burst of speed or a pause between them leaves its slope unchanged.

explain.text:
An average rate of change says how much one thing changed for each unit of another, between two points. You already work these out. 120 km in 2 hours is 120 ÷ 2 = 60 km per hour, the change in distance divided by the change in time, and its unit comes straight from the division, km over hours.

A boat leaving a buoy at a steady 4 metres a second is 4x metres away after x seconds. A rule like this, which takes one number and gives back one, is a [[function]], written f(x) = 4x and read "f of x". f(3) means the rule applied to 3, so f(3) = 4 × 3 = 12 m. On its graph, pick two points, P at 1 s and Q at 3 s, and join them with a straight line, a [[chord]]. Δ, the Greek letter delta, means "change in". From P to Q, Δx = 3 − 1 = 2 s and Δy = 12 − 4 = 8 m, so Δy ÷ Δx = 8 m ÷ 2 s = 4 m per s, the slope of the chord. On a straight line every chord gives the same answer, because each second adds the same 4 m, so Δy is 4 times Δx wherever the points sit. A second boat that started 10 m out, f(x) = 10 + 4x, has the same slope, 4 m per s. Dividing its y by its x at 5 s gives 30 ÷ 5 = 6 m per s, which is too much, because the 30 m includes the 10 m it had before the clock started. y ÷ x is the slope of the line from (0, 0), so it answers a different question unless your first point is (0, 0).

A boat pulling away from the quay speeds up, so its graph curves. Say it covers f(x) = x² metres in x seconds, where x² means x × x, the area of a square x long on each side. It covers 1 m in its first second, 3 m in its second, 5 m in its third and 7 m in its fourth, more each second, so a chord further along rises more for the same Δx. From 0 s to 1 s the chord's slope is 1 m per s, and from 3 s to 4 s it is 16 − 9 = 7 m per s. Chords in different places generally no longer agree, so the answer depends on which two points you pick. Δy ÷ Δx between them is the [[average rate of change]] over that stretch, the change in f divided by the change in x.[^1] It is the steady rate that would give the same change, because that rate times Δx gives back Δy. From 0 s to 4 s the curve and the steady boat's line both go from 0 m to 16 m, so both chords give 4 m per s, though one boat crawled at first and then went faster. An average does not show what happened between its two points. Calculus uses the slope of a chord like this to estimate the rate at which one quantity changes in relation to another.[^2]

A falling graph gives a rate below zero. A tank draining from 200 L at 0 min to 50 L at 5 min has Δy = 50 − 200 = −150 L, because the later amount is the smaller, so the rate is −150 ÷ 5 = −30 L per min, and the minus says it is emptying. Take both changes in the same order, or the sign comes out wrong. Your electro-technology papers use Δ the same way: an inductor's emf is written e = LΔi/Δt,[^5] where Δi ÷ Δt is the change in current divided by the change in time, in amps per second. **The average rate of change between two points is Δy ÷ Δx, the change in y divided by the change in x,[^1] the slope of the chord joining them, in units of y per unit of x.**

analogy.text: Your electricity meter reads 1,250 kWh at 8 am and 1,262 kWh at 2 pm. Δy is 12 kWh over Δx of 6 hours, so the average power is 12 ÷ 6 = 2 kW. A steady 2 kW load would move the meter the same 12 kWh, whatever the kettle and the heater did in between.
analogy.breaks: kWh per hour tidies into kW, a unit with its own name, which most rates, such as litres per minute, do not have. And a meter that only records energy used can only go up, so on its own it has no falling graph and no minus rate, as a draining tank has.

practice.text:
- Pick the two points and read each one's x and y, with their units.
- Find Δy and Δx, taking both in the same order, later minus earlier.
- Divide Δy by Δx.
- Give the unit, the y unit per x unit.
- Check that the rate times Δx gives back Δy, and that a falling graph gave a minus.

**Rules of thumb:** Change over change, so subtract first, then divide. On a curve the answer depends on the two points, so say which two you used.

**Worked example:** A day tank reads 900 L at 06:00 and 660 L at 10:00. Δy = 660 − 900 = −240 L and Δx = 10 − 6 = 4 h, so the average rate is −240 ÷ 4 = −60 L per hour, and the minus says it is emptying. Check: −60 L per hour for 4 hours is −240 L. The MCA's Second Engineer maths syllabus asks for this same working, as determining the gradient of a chord,[^3] gradient being another word for slope.

**Common mistakes**
One calculus teacher reports that almost all his students, even at the start of calculus, can work out a rate at an instant, but almost no one gives him the correct average rate.[^4] These are the slips to check for.
- Dividing y by x. For the tank, 660 ÷ 10 = 66 L per hour divides by the clock time, not by a change in it.
- Dividing Δx by Δy. 4 ÷ (−240) gives hours per litre, and the unit gives it away.
- Dropping the minus. +60 L per hour would say the tank is filling.
- Averaging the readings. (900 + 660) ÷ 2 = 780 L is an amount, not a rate.

interactive.html:
Drag two points along a graph and watch how steep the straight line between them is.

The rules and readings are examples, chosen to keep the numbers whole.

checks.label: The average rate of change over an interval is the ratio of the amount of change in the function to the corresponding change in x: on every chord screen, for every pair of points P and Q it can show, the working reads (f(Q) − f(P)) ÷ (Q − P) in the y unit per x unit, and so does the drawing at its end and after a drag
Determines the gradient of a chord: on every chord screen the chord is drawn as a straight line from P to Q, and its gradient on the drawing, read back through the axes, is the slope in the working

On the straight line f(x) = 4x every chord gives 4 m per s, and the boat that started 10 m out gives 4 m per s from 1 s to 5 s (30 − 14 = 16 m over 4 s, where 30 ÷ 5 would give 6); on f(x) = x² the boat covers 1, 3, 5 and 7 m in its first four seconds, so its chords differ: 1 m per s from 0 s to 1 s, 3 from 1 s to 2 s, 7 from 3 s to 4 s and 6 from 2 s to 4 s, while from 0 s to 4 s both graphs give 4 m per s
The tank's rule gives 200 L at 0 min, 128 L at 2 min, 50 L at 5 min, 32 L at 6 min and 0 L at 10 min, so its chords give −30, −24 and −10 L per min, and every chord on its falling graph gives a minus
The example readings give 66 − 30 = 36 °C over 40 − 10 = 30 min, 1.2 °C per min, and 12 − 6 = 6 V over 4 s, 1.5 V per s, as the working under each table's graph says

Every puzzle offers three different answers and accepts only the right one; each wrong answer is the slip it stands for, worked from the same points: 70 m and 19 m against 30 m; 6 m per s and 0.25 s per m against 4 m per s; 10 m and 4 m per s against 6 m per s; +24 L per min and −96 L against −24 L per min; 0.67 s per V and 2 V per s against 1.5 V per s; and 0 and +10 L per min against −10 L per min

Before an answer no puzzle shows its answer: the working ends in a question mark, the triangle's sides read only Δx and Δy, and nothing is red; a right answer ends the working in it with nothing red, and every wrong answer shows its slip in red
Dragging keeps each point on a whole number inside the axes, with P always left of Q
Every demonstration has finished arriving within 4.5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion, right or wrong, within 1.3 s

applied.problem: The lesson defines a chord as a line joining two points on the graph, but for f(x) = 10 + 4x the point (0, 0) is not on the graph, so the line from (0, 0) to (5 s, 30 m) is not a chord; call it a line.
The quote is about the teacher's own students ("almost everyone, even at the start of Calculus I"), not everyone starting calculus; keep its narrower group.
